speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, I seek to move, “That the total sum to be allocated for Head F of the Estimates be reduced by $100”.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To that end, it is notable that questions posed by MPs to one Ministry may be redirected to be answered by another Ministry, without prior reference to the MP.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From my understanding, such redirection is done by the Government Ministries and not the Parliamentary staff.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Of course, sometimes the redirection is justified, such as when the MP may have inadvertently asked the question to the wrong Ministry, for example, questions about banks may be mistakenly filed with the Ministry of Finance (MOF) when the bank regulator, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), comes within the province of the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, it seems to me that questions may also be redirected simply because the Government finds it expedient to do so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This may undermine the main purpose of Question Time – Government accountability.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To take a recent example, the Leader of Opposition (LO) had in August last year filed a PQ to the Ministry of Transport (MOT) asking for the Land Transport Authority’s (LTA) assessment on the demand for bus services on the routes being plied by the special shuttle bus services at Marine Parade Group Representation Constituency.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even though his question asked for LTA’s assessment of transport needs, his question was redirected to the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) without his input.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When he rose to ask supplementary questions which were transport-related, the Minister of State for MCCY was unable to answer them and instead invited the LO to file a question with LTA instead, notwithstanding the fact that the LO had initially done so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the Minister for Transport did step in shortly at that session to address the LO’s queries, the question still remains as to why a question posed to LTA was redirected to MCCY in the first place.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: MPs compete to have their questions chosen for priority listing, failing which they either let it lapse for written answer or hope to have priority listing on another day.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When a question is redirected to a Ministry that cannot address the MP’s concerns, the MP may face procedural objections to refiling it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, on the reputation of Parliament as an institution that makes laws prospectively and with advanced notice to the public before implementation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Workers’ Party (WP) expressed serious misgivings about the proposed acquisition of Income Insurance by Allianz, but we did not support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As my party colleague, Ms He Ting Ru, had argued then, the legislation affected a live transaction and would undermine legal and business certainty that was critical to a business hub such as Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In that debate, Deputy Speaker Christopher de Souza opined that the Bill was a hybrid Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He explained that although the provisions of the Bill were drafted in general terms, it was clear that the Bill was, in substance, aimed at the proposed acquisition of Income by Allianz.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Ordinarily, the Standing Orders would require that such a Bill be referred to a Select Committee for close scrutiny, since it affected prejudicially the rights of particular parties.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But because a Certificate of Urgency was obtained, the Select Committee procedure was done away with.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This deprived Parliament of the opportunity to hear from the affected parties themselves before passing the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, the urgent Bill could have been avoided had the lacuna in MCCY’s regulatory ambit been identified in 2022, when Income’s corporatisation exercise was approved.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In 1966, a Constitutional Commission was chaired by then Chief Justice Wee Chong Jin and it recommended the formation of the PCMR, which was established in 1970.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Its role is to scrutinise Bills passed by Parliament for any differentiating measures that discriminate against any racial or religious community, and if so found, to refer the Bill back to Parliament for reconsideration.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The PCMR was later entrusted with other functions as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Wee Chong Jin Commission had recommended that the PCMR members be chosen from distinguished individuals who did not hold any political affiliation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It also recommended that members serve for fixed terms that could be renewed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, these recommendations were not adopted and today, the PCMR is comprised of 18 members, five of whom are appointed permanently and for life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am very disturbed, Sir, that all five permanent members in the PCMR have been or still are Cabinet Ministers, including currently, Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong and the incumbent Minister for Home Affairs and Law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Of the five, only Mr Abdullah Tarmugi and Mr S Dhanabalan received their permanent appointments after they left the Cabinet.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, most of the Bills passed by Parliament are proposed by the Government, and yet the Bills are being sent for scrutiny by a PCMR consisting of life members of incumbent and former Cabinet Ministers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If it is the case that the PCMR would benefit from hearing from the Government, the Prime Minister is already empowered to authorise any member of the Cabinet to participate in PCMR meetings, albeit without a vote.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even so, it does not explain why they have to be appointed for life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Whether or not it works today will not be indicative of whether it works tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And a system which entrenches the influence of members of former administrations, until quite literally, the day they die, in my opinion, is not a viable one.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Member for her cut.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: One, on the way Question Time was managed, but essentially, that cut was really focused on redirection of questions; the second, was on the reputation of Parliament, but essentially, that focused, I think, more on Bills brought on an urgent basis, and Certificate of Urgency in the specific context of the NTUC-Allianz Bill; and the third, was on the PCMR, which actually does not quite fall into the gist of the cut that was filed, because it says, "Question time and the legislative process need to be safeguarded and strengthened".

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And I am afraid there was not sufficient indication that PCMR was going to be part of that.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But nevertheless, I will address the question as it has been presented and if there are any further details that are needed or if the Member thinks is not fully addressed, the Member can let me know.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the at the end of the day, what is the purpose of PQs?

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The purpose of PQs is so that Members can ask questions about things and the Ministers can reply.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is really for the Government to assess and determine who would be in the best position to respond to the questions.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And in some cases, MPs actually do address the question to the wrong Ministry.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, MOF frequently gets PQs on the MAS.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MAS reports to the PMO, not to MOF.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, essentially, when the PQs come in, Parliament will look at that and they will send it to the Ministry that is named.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And the Ministry that is named will have to look to see whether this is under the Ministry's purview or whether another Ministry is best-placed or is the policy owner or has the carriage of the operational aspects.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, that is something you should leave to the Government to determine.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is not really for the MP to decide who has the relevant knowledge.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is for the Government, looking at the question, to determine who amongst us, who amongst the agencies and the Ministries is the one responsible or has the knowledge or is in the best position to respond.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What is truly important, at the end of the day, is that the question is responded to.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Because no matter who the question is redirected to, which agency or which Ministry, there will be an answer provided.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And if, at the end of the day, the answer from the Minister or Ministry is not sufficient, the MPs do have the opportunity to come back and to ask further questions in another PQ or on another occasion.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think in the example that Ms Lim cited of the Leader of the Opposition's (LO's) PQ that was filed, addressed to the Ministry of Transport (MOT), asking for LTA's assessment.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: My understanding is that, the bus decision, in this particular case, was made by the People's Association (PA), not MOT or LTA.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And it was, therefore, not for MOT to explain why the shuttle bus was launched, because that was a scheme done under PA.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And PA is a statutory board that comes under MCCY.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That is why the Minister for MCCY responded to that.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That said, I believe the Minister for Transport Chee Hong Tat did rise to clarify a point from LO as he had asked with respect to the Bus Connectivity Enhancement Programme, and that comes under MOT.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, because that one came under MOT, the Minister for Transport responded to that.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, that deals with the first issue, which is on redirection.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Then, the second thing on the reputation of Parliament, let me just say at the outset that actually just bringing a Bill quickly on a Certificate of Urgency is not the most important consideration when it comes to reputation of Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The reputation of Parliament, what is most important is that MPs conduct themselves with the highest standards of conduct, with integrity, do not mislead people outside as to what happened in Parliament and also speak the truth to Parliament and its Committees.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The issue that Ms Lim raised was Bills which are presented on an urgent basis.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our system ensures that Members do have sufficient time to review the Bills and to debate them robustly in this House.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, there may be situations where it is necessary for a Bill to be brought for Second Reading at short notice.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Hence, our system also allows for a Bill to be presented under a Certificate of Urgency on the rare occasions when there is a need to do so.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On the Bills that were presented under Certificates of Urgency during this term of Government, there was the COVID-19 Temporary Measures Bill and the three amendment Bills thereafter, as well as the other COVID-19-related Bills.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Then we had the one that Ms Lim talked about, which was the Insurance (Amendment) Bill in October 2024.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This was necessary because the proposed deal by Allianz was under active consideration by NTUC Income shareholders at the time.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A long duration between the First Reading and the Second Reading of the Bill, and thus, a delay in the amended law taking effect, would have given rise to even more uncertainty in the market and for the parties concerned.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Minister Edwin Tong had explained this context in his Ministerial Statement when the Bill was introduced.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But from time to time, there may be exceptional circumstances, such as in the case of the Allianz Bill, that call for us to be an agile legislature so that we can best serve Singaporeans.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I come now to the last point which Ms Lim raised, which I understand, really, to be an objection to the fact that the PCMR has certain permanent members.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There is value in having members who are also members of Cabinet because they provide a certain perspective.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are other members, of course, who come in, and those members may change or provide other perspectives.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But what we try to do, particularly with minority rights, is to have a wide spectrum and a wide range.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I will give you some time, yes, but I hope not too long.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We are actually approaching the end of guillotine time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have three clarifications for the Minister based on the three topics which are raised.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First, on the Government deciding which Ministry should answer the question, does the Leader of the House not agree that sometimes questions can cut across more than one Ministry and the MP actually would be the one to know what is the focus of the question.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And, therefore, is it not possible for there to be a procedure where there is some loop back to the MP to ask the MP, "Alright, we intend to redirect it to another Ministry.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Do you have any concerns about it?" Then, at least, our input can be taken into account.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second topic I raised on legislative process, actually, I think the Leader of the House kind of missed the main issue, which was that, as pointed out by the Deputy Speaker at that Sitting, the Insurance (Amendment) Bill was a hybrid Bill that directly affected particular parties.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And under the Standing Orders, it is supposed to be the norm that if there are such Bills, then a Select Committee has to be formed so that Parliament can hear directly from the affected parties on how the proposed Bill would affect them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In this situation, we are talking about a really important social issue and the MPs were deprived of that opportunity to hear from the parties because the Certificate of Urgency was issued.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And therefore, the Bills were just passed without the Select Committee procedure being activated.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I think, to that extent, Parliament has been prejudiced.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Actually, what the Minister answered was already pre-empted in my speech.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: She said that having members with knowledge of why particular Bills were passed or the legislative history would be helpful to PCMR.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But the Constitution already provides for the Prime Minister to appoint Ministers to attend PCMR meetings to give that perspective to PCMR members.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, there is no need for Ministers to be members of PCMR for their voices to be heard.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Does she not agree with me that the system design, if PCMR is supposed to be an independent check on legislation, having Ministers on PCMR actually does not look quite right?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the PCMR, I am not sure that the PCMR is set up as a check on the legislature.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is set up as a check to ensure that minority rights are addressed or thought about.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Whether you appoint members or whether they are permanent members, the point is that, they have something valuable to contribute.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, when the Standing Orders were designed, this was thought about.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And you do anticipate that there may be such situations that are urgent.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that is why a Certificate of Urgency was brought.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in other words, it is not that every day we have Certificates of Urgency.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this particular instance, there was a need to do it quickly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that was already explained by Minister Edwin Tong, so it is unnecessary for me to go into that in detail.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, on the last one about redirection, I think we would not want to put in place a process that for every single question that is filed, you have to go back to an MP and check what their underlying intent was.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I mean, really, MPs, when they file their questions, should make their questions clear.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the situation that Ms Lim describes, where the question is redirected and the Member feels that it should not be because the underlying intent was to ask the other Ministry something, the Member is always free to reach out to the relevant Minister and explain that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Actually, usually what happens is, when we get a PQ that is not very clear, the Ministries or either the Senior Parliamentary Secretary or the Minister of State will reach out to the MP to ask, "What exactly are you asking here?" There have been cases where we have had to do that because the intent of the PQ is not clear.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It does not happen all the time, but, sometimes, when the question is ambiguously worded, we do.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In that instance, once we ascertain from the MP, what the real intent is, we can then decide whether to leave it with one Ministry or redirect it to another.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But on the face of it, questions ought to be clear if they are properly drafted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And if it is clear and it appears to us that this falls under the purview of a particular agency or Ministry, we will redirect it accordingly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Like I said, it is not as though the MP has no chance to come back and file a clearer PQ directed at the Ministry or agency that the Member wants.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Lim, would you like to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, that decision, sometimes there is a tussle between the relevant officers and Members about this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And last of all, regarding the urgency of the Insurance (Amendment) Bill, of course, to note that the deal has been aborted, so I do not know whether the parties felt that they were inadequately listened to, so I do not know the answer to that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But, Sir, in any event, there are clearly many interesting issues that we can talk about Parliament and its functioning.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And I would hope that there is common cause that all of us want Parliament to be effective.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And with that, Sir, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, if the Member has any clarifications on that, that is something to be directed to Minister Edwin Tong.
